\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These pitfalls establish that single-method, single-regime analyses---the current default---cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our multi-method consensus framework addresses this fragility by requiring convergent evidence across multiple independent methods and random seeds.
Calibrated on effect-size reference pairs with a non-circular 4-method panel, the framework achieves FNR${=}$0\% with permutation Granger power${=}1.0$, and four tiers of practical guidance scaling from exploratory screening to publication-grade claims.

Applying the framework, token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse, Tier~3 across 4~seeds and GPT-2-medium replication) with a consistent one-generation lead; at $\alpha{=}0.75$, directional asymmetry is confirmed (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse across 3~seeds) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), mapping the detectability boundary.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

The methodological pitfalls we expose arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series, and we conjecture the consensus framework transfers to other iterative training settings where multiple detection methods can be applied in parallel.
Limitations are detailed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}; future directions are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	Several limitations constrain the generalizability of our findings.
5	
6	\paragraph{Model scale.}
7	Our primary experiments use Pythia-410M (410M parameters); preliminary cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters).
8	Both are decoder-only transformers of similar scale, small by contemporary standards.
9	Whether the entropy-leads-diversity pattern and the consensus framework's operating thresholds hold at billion-parameter scale remains untested.
10	The batch size difference between architectures (4 for Pythia vs.\ 32 for GPT-2-medium) means each training step exposes $8\times$ more data in the latter, potentially accelerating collapse dynamics without altering the qualitative pattern.
11	
12	\paragraph{Data domain.}
13	Training data is drawn from a single domain (a WikiText-103 subset), and domain-specific distributional properties---vocabulary richness, syntactic complexity, topical diversity---may influence the coupling between canary and downstream metrics.
14	Domains with inherently low diversity (e.g., legal text, code) could exhibit different canary dynamics.
15	
16	\paragraph{Short time series ($T{=}10$).}
17	With 11 data points per series, our statistical analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
18	This limits power for all methods and makes the Toda--Yamamoto procedure particularly unreliable (power estimated at 0.05--0.20 for our effect sizes).
19	Longer generation chains would improve statistical power but impose substantial computational cost.
20	
21	\paragraph{Bivariate Granger $\neq$ causality.}
22	Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders.
23	An unobserved process---such as a latent shift in the training data distribution---could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations.
24	Our multi-method consensus framework mitigates but does not eliminate this limitation; multivariate VAR models would be required to test for confounders directly.
25	
26	\paragraph{Regime boundary uncertainty.}
27	The detectability boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$--$0.75$ is characterized with limited resolution (five $\alpha$ levels).
28	Whether this boundary is sharp (phase-transition-like) or gradual, and whether it shifts with model scale or data properties, remains open.
29	Three-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.75$ confirms directional asymmetry (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), leaving the exact boundary position uncertain.
30	
31	\paragraph{No intervention experiment.}
32	We observe that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse but do not test whether acting on canary signals (e.g., halting training or reducing $\alpha$) can prevent or delay collapse onset.
33	Without intervention evidence, the practical value of the canary remains theoretical.
34	
35	\paragraph{Replace-only protocol.}
36	Our experiments use replace-only data accumulation; accumulate-mode training~\cite{dey2024breaking,kazdan2025collapse} may exhibit qualitatively different canary dynamics or eliminate the need for canary monitoring entirely~\cite{falahati2026curated}.
37	
38	\paragraph{Scope limited to diversity metrics.}
39	Our canary claims are scoped to distinct-$n$ diversity metrics~\cite{li2016diversity}---not to model collapse broadly~\cite{schaeffer2025position}---as the perplexity channel proved spurious after differencing.
40	This scoping is theoretically motivated by the calibration-diversity tradeoff~\cite{cao2025entropycal}, but means our findings may not generalize to other collapse manifestations (e.g., factual degradation, reasoning capability loss).

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Training language models on their own output across successive generations leads to progressive distribution degradation, a phenomenon variously termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse} or Model Autophagy Disorder~\cite{alemohammad2024mad}.
5	Tail modes vanish, lexical diversity narrows, and calibration deteriorates as each generation's output becomes the next generation's training data.
6	As large language models become ubiquitous content generators, the fraction of machine-generated text on the web grows steadily, making iterative training collapse---where models are unwittingly trained on the output of earlier model generations---a practical concern for the long-term stability of language model ecosystems.
7	
8	A natural follow-up question is whether cheap-to-compute statistics---\emph{canary metrics}---can provide early warning of impending collapse, analogous to early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological and climate systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}.
9	Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} informally observe that expected calibration error rises before accuracy degrades; SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators of distributional shift; and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
10	Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims---whether a canary metric genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---has received little scrutiny.
11	
12	We identify several methodological deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse:
13	(1)~no differencing tests to rule out spurious regression arising from shared non-stationary trends---a well-known hazard when correlating co-trending time series;
14	(2)~no multi-method cross-validation---conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose implicit assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined;
15	(3)~no multiple comparison correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg FDR control), increasing the risk of false discoveries when testing many metric pairs simultaneously; and
16	(4)~no regime-dependent analysis, despite the possibility that the same statistical test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
17	The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
18	Their analysis, however, is limited to a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and reports informal visual comparisons without statistical tests---leaving open the question of whether the observed lead is genuine or an artifact of shared trends.
19	The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}---widely adopted in ecology for anticipating tipping points---provides the theoretical motivation for canary-based prediction, but has not been systematically applied to iterative training collapse with the methodological rigor that short, noisy time series demand~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
20	
21	We address these gaps through a systematic case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse---the progressive loss of lexical diversity in model-generated text across training generations.
22	Using Pythia-410M across five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we expose three methodological pitfalls that undermine naive lead-lag analysis:

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training language models on their own output across successive generations leads to progressive distribution degradation, a phenomenon variously termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse} or Model Autophagy Disorder~\cite{alemohammad2024mad}.
Tail modes vanish, lexical diversity narrows, and calibration deteriorates as each generation's output becomes the next generation's training data.
As large language models become ubiquitous content generators, the fraction of machine-generated text on the web grows steadily, making iterative training collapse---where models are unwittingly trained on the output of earlier model generations---a practical concern for the long-term stability of language model ecosystems.

A natural follow-up question is whether cheap-to-compute statistics---\emph{canary metrics}---can provide early warning of impending collapse, analogous to early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological and climate systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} informally observe that expected calibration error rises before accuracy degrades; SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators of distributional shift; and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims---whether a canary metric genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---has received little scrutiny.

We identify several methodological deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse:
(1)~no differencing tests to rule out spurious regression arising from shared non-stationary trends---a well-known hazard when correlating co-trending time series;
(2)~no multi-method cross-validation---conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose implicit assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined;
(3)~no multiple comparison correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg FDR control), increasing the risk of false discoveries when testing many metric pairs simultaneously; and
(4)~no regime-dependent analysis, despite the possibility that the same statistical test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, is limited to a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and reports informal visual comparisons without statistical tests---leaving open the question of whether the observed lead is genuine or an artifact of shared trends.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}---widely adopted in ecology for anticipating tipping points---provides the theoretical motivation for canary-based prediction, but has not been systematically applied to iterative training collapse with the methodological rigor that short, noisy time series demand~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We address these gaps through a systematic case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse---the progressive loss of lexical diversity in model-generated text across training generations.
Using Pythia-410M across five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we expose three methodological pitfalls that undermine naive lead-lag analysis:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Method sensitivity.} Applied to the same data (16 candidate canary$\to$downstream pairs, including candidates later excluded; \S\ref{sec:case_study}), five lead-lag detection methods yield FDR significance rates ranging from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 25\% (Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality), with inter-method agreement of Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.185$ (poor agreement).
    \item \textbf{Spurious regression.} Canary$\to$perplexity associations appear near-universal in undifferenced analysis but vanish entirely after first-differencing ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), revealing them as artifacts of co-trending rather than genuine temporal precedence.
    \item \textbf{Regime dependence.} Permutation Granger tests find 24/24 canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant at full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$) but 0/8 at $\alpha{\leq}0.50$, demonstrating that detectability depends sharply on the contamination level.
\end{enumerate}
To move beyond single-method analysis, we propose a multi-method consensus framework with empirically calibrated thresholds, requiring agreement across multiple independent statistical methods and random seeds before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust.

The framework's utility is demonstrated by its calibration on built-in experimental controls.
Naive cross-correlation identifies 100\% of canary--collapse metric pairs as FDR-significant; the consensus pipeline (requiring ${\geq}4/5$ methods and ${\geq}3/4$ seeds) retains only those pairs meeting effect-size criteria calibrated against the null control.
On reference extremes, the framework achieves a false positive rate of 0\% at the $\alpha{=}0.0$ null control (single seed) (where individual methods reach up to 100\% FPR) and a false negative rate of 0\% against six effect-size reference pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
Applying the framework, we identify token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$, validated by the full consensus pipeline, with cross-correlation $|r|{>}0.99$ and directional asymmetry confirmed by 0/24 reverse-direction FDR-significant pairs; three-seed directional replication at $\alpha{=}0.75$ confirms asymmetry (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse via permutation Granger), while method-level consensus remains in the transitional regime (Tier~2--3), consistent with a detectability boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$--$0.75$.
We note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Systematic exposure of three methodological pitfalls} (method sensitivity, spurious regression, regime dependence) in lead-lag analysis of iterative training collapse.
    Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%; first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely; and the same Granger test shifts from 24/24 FDR-significant pairs to 0/8 across contamination levels.
    These results demonstrate that single-method, single-regime analyses---the current norm in this literature---are unreliable.

    \item \textbf{A multi-method consensus framework} that instantiates known statistical methods in a novel sequential pipeline with empirical calibration, achieving FNR${=}$0\% on effect-size reference pairs (4-method panel, permutation Granger power${=}1.0$) with four-tier practical guidance.

    \item \textbf{Identification of token entropy as a robust one-generation-ahead canary} for diversity collapse at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, confirmed by 4 independent methods, 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium, with complete directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse). The claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), a case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), and consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications---including the practical utility paradox, the token entropy--perplexity distinction, and NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis---and outlines directions for future work.
\S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across five contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha{=}0.75$ and $\alpha{=}0.25$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; other conditions use seed~42.

We track two \emph{canary metrics}---cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}---and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.

\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:method_sensitivity}

We open with Claim~3---method sensitivity---because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.

\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{4/16} (25.0\%).
Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 25\%}: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
The spurious-signal rate---the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative---is \textbf{75\%} across all five methods and \textbf{62.5\%} when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.

\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.

\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
At $d_{\max}{=}0$ (most permissive), approximately 6\% of pairs are rejected; at adaptive $d_{\max}$ determined by ADF unit-root tests, 75\%; at $d_{\max}{=}1$ (most conservative), \textbf{94\%}.
This single hyperparameter swings conclusions from near-universal significance to near-universal non-significance.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$: from $\sim$6\% rejection at $d_{\max}{=}0$ to 94\% at $d_{\max}{=}1$, demonstrating that this single hyperparameter can reverse conclusions about temporal precedence.}
\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation and Toda--Yamamoto, which anchor the permissive and conservative extremes respectively) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (no synthetic data, serving as null control), naive cross-correlation finds \textbf{100\%} of pairs significant---a textbook spurious-regression outcome in trending time series.
Permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto correctly find 0\%.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, correlation-based methods (naive, differenced, threshold) unanimously find significance while causal methods unanimously find non-significance (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), the most extreme method$\times$regime divergence in our experiments.

\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}

Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.

Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.

\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
\label{sec:case_study}

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.

\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 19/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics---a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE performs equivalently to token entropy across four of five methods (naive, differenced, threshold, permutation Granger).
Its classification as ``secondary'' is driven entirely by Toda--Yamamoto Type~II errors at $T{=}10$, where bootstrap power analysis yields estimated power of 0.05--0.20 depending on $d_{\max}$.
Resolving ECE's true canary status requires longer time series.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).% provenance: gen_wiki_gpt2m_a025_s42
The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).


\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
\label{sec:consensus_validation}

We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
At $\alpha{=}0.0$, no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation: 8/8 pairs) through 62.5\% (threshold) and 37.5\% (differenced) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto).
The consensus framework at $K{\geq}4/5$ achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%}, matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
Toda--Yamamoto alone yields FNR${=}$33.3\% (2/6), missing ECE$\to$distinct-2 and ECE$\to$distinct-3 due to Type~II errors at $T{=}10$.
We note a design asymmetry: FPR is validated on method-only data (single seed at $\alpha{=}0.0$), while FNR uses method$\times$seed joint data (4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
Full joint calibration---multi-seed null-control experiments---remains future work.
Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.

Permutation Granger achieves power${=}1.0$ on genuine pairs (canary$\to$diversity) and power${=}0.0$ on spurious pairs (canary$\to$perplexity), providing clean separation.
Toda--Yamamoto achieves power${=}0.05$--$0.20$ on genuine pairs (depending on $d_{\max}$), confirming its poor sensitivity at $T{=}10$.
